features: Fixed — REOPENING A CREDIT NOTE FOR EDITING FLIPPED THE SIGN OF ITS AMOUNTS ON SAVE. A credit note of €1,000.00 plus VAT, reopened to correct a date or a reference and saved again without touching the amounts, went from −€1,220.00 to +€1,220.00 in the database: it stopped being a credit and became an expense, and the debt towards the supplier grew by twice as much instead of shrinking. A credit note's money is stored already negative — it is the original recording that applies the minus sign, once — but the edit form handed those negatives straight back to the server, and saving applied the sign a second time: minus times minus makes plus.

No database changes in this version: no migrations and no data corrected retroactively. A flipped credit note can be identified with certainty, because it is a credit note with a positive total and that cannot exist: it is put right by reversing it and recording it again.

Fixed — RECORDING A PAYMENT COULD SHOW AN ERROR PAGE INSTEAD OF A MESSAGE. Every payment can carry a key that guards against double submission: if the same request arrives twice — a double click, a network timeout that makes the browser retry — the system recognises the key and returns the payment already recorded instead of creating a second one. That key, however, is unique across ALL accounting entries, not just payments: internal transfers use it too. If it belonged to a movement that was not a payment, the system had nothing to return and stopped with a technical error no screen knows how to explain; if it belonged to another building's payment, it returned that one silently, suggesting the save had succeeded while nothing had been recorded for the current building. These are now two distinct cases, each with its own message, and both are resolved by regenerating the key. A genuine double submission still behaves as before: no duplicate payment.

Fixed — A PHP WARNING APPEARED WHEN RECORDING A PRIOR-PERIOD INVOICE. On prior-period invoices the funding source is optional — a historical debt can be recorded without stating where it will be covered from — but two of the three coverage types, «Instalment 0» and «Reserve fund», read it as if it were always present. The third was already fine. Recording still succeeded, but left a warning in the logs for every invoice, and on an installation configured to display errors on screen the warning ended up in front of the administrator in the middle of a perfectly successful operation. Neither of these two clean-ups came from a report: both surfaced while using the product to populate the example data.

Touching the amounts was not required: opening the credit note for editing and saving was enough. And nothing prevented it — an open credit note is editable like any other invoice, and the amount validation accepts negative numbers without objection.
Recording a new credit note was never affected: there the figures are typed positive and the system applies the sign, which is exactly the behaviour editing has now been realigned to.

Why no check had caught it: the accounting entry still balanced perfectly, because the filter that swaps DEBIT and CREDIT on credit notes was applied anyway and the two columns stayed equal. What changed was which side the accounts sat on — the cost went back among expenses instead of offsetting them — not the balance between debit and credit. It is the same shape as the previous version's defect: a symmetrical error is invisible to double-entry.

Worth knowing: now that a credit note's amounts reach the form as positive figures, the budget overrun check counts them as it would an expense, and a credit note may raise the «saving over budget» warning. This is not new to this version — it already happens when recording a new credit note, where the amounts have always been positive. The fix aligns editing with recording rather than letting them diverge.

The defect is pinned from both sides. A JavaScript test mounts the edit screen and checks the number that ends up in the amount box, because the error lived in the form's initialisation. A PHP test pins the server's contract: that a credit note is born negative, that it really is editable — were a guard to stop it, the defect would be unreachable — and that opening and re-saving twice in a row does not make the sign oscillate. A further test checks that an ordinary invoice has not changed behaviour.
